opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a fun question, because looking back it wasn't a carefully planned move.

When I was first doing research, I was working on problems in communications, including some of the quantum side. It was intellectually beautiful: very mathematical, very elegant. But at some point I realized I wanted to work on something where I could *see* the result. In communications you improve a bound, you get a better error rate, and it's meaningful, but it's abstract. With vision, you run your algorithm and there's an image or a video in front of you. You immediately know whether it works or whether it's garbage. That tight feedback loop really appealed to me.

There was also a sense that vision was wide open. Getting a machine to understand what it's looking at felt like one of the fundamental questions of intelligence, and nobody had solved it. Humans do it effortlessly, and computers were terrible at it. That gap felt exciting rather than intimidating.

And honestly, the math transferred more than people might think. Signal processing, probability, optimization, estimation under noise: those carry straight over. So it didn't feel like starting from zero. It felt like taking the tools I had and pointing them at a problem that was more tangible and, to me, more fun.

Of course, I didn't know then that deep learning was about to change everything. Later, when generative models came along, it felt like the field went from understanding images to actually creating them. But the original pull was simple. I wanted to work on something I could see, something that felt connected to how intelligence actually works.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a grand plan. When I was an undergraduate in Taiwan, I was studying electrical engineering, and quantum communications felt like the most exciting frontier at the time. It was elegant, very mathematical, and I liked that. But when I actually started doing research in it, I realized something about myself: I wanted to build things I could see working. Quantum communication experiments were extremely slow to run, the hardware was fragile, and you could spend months on a setup that produced one data point. I respected it, but it didn't fit my temperament.

Around the same time, I took a course on image processing, and I remember the first time I wrote a simple algorithm that detected edges in a photo. It was trivial by today's standards, but the feedback loop was immediate. You write the code, you run it, you look at the output, and you can tell right away whether your idea was right or wrong. That immediacy was addictive to me.

The other thing was the problem itself. Making a machine understand what it sees seemed like one of the deepest questions you could ask, and at the time, around the mid-2000s, nobody really knew how to do it well. The field was wide open. So when I went to the University of Maryland for my PhD and worked with Rama Chellappa, I committed to vision fully. A lot of the mathematical tools I learned from the physics side, the probability, the linear algebra, the optimization, turned out to be very useful. So I don't think of it as leaving one field for another. I think of it as taking the tools I had and pointing them at a problem that I found more alive.

astra-6.text:
What drew me to computer vision was the idea of getting computers to understand the visual world. With quantum communications, I was working on very abstract questions. In vision, you could take an image, develop an algorithm, and see what it could—or couldn’t—understand. That made the research feel very tangible to me.

There was also this fascinating gap: seeing feels effortless for us, but it’s remarkably difficult to teach a machine to do it. I wanted to understand that gap and build systems that could close it. That curiosity pulled me toward computer vision.

sol-6.1.text: The common thread for me was an interest in how we represent and process information. In quantum communications, I was thinking about how information is transmitted. Computer vision brought me to a different question: how can a machine extract meaning from an image? I found that very compelling. We recognize objects and understand scenes so naturally, but getting a computer to do that forces you to ask what understanding actually requires. That combination of fundamental questions and tangible results drew me toward vision.
